About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Visual Arts – Photography Years 12–
13 of the New Zealand Curriculum.
Progress and assessment information for Visual Arts – Photography Years 12–13 is
still in development. Once that is completed, Visual Arts – Photography Years 12–13
is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum
Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.
It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Visual Arts – Photography Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in
Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.
This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.




Visual Arts – Photography | Years 12–13 | October 2026                                  Page 2

Purpose statement
                                                                        Te toi whakairo, ka ihiihi, ka wehiwehi, ka aweawe te   Artistic excellence makes the world sit up in
                                                                        ao katoa.                                               wonder.




  In Visual Arts – Photography, students are taught how photographic images are
  created, interpreted, and used to communicate ideas. They learn how lens-based
  processes, visual language, and photographic conventions can be applied to
  investigate, develop, and communicate meaning through purposeful image-
  making. Students experiment with composition, exposure, lighting, sequencing,
  and image manipulation while developing increasingly independent artistic
  practice.

Students are taught photographic concepts, processes, and techniques, and how to
select and use cameras, equipment, lighting, materials, and digital technologies with
increasing control and precision. They develop knowledge of how photographic
decisions influence meaning and communication, and how visual language is used
intentionally to create original photographic imagery.
Photography provides students with the knowledge and practices to investigate,
analyse, evaluate, and apply understanding through sustained photographic
investigation. Students engage with contexts such as cultural, social, historical, and
contemporary, examining established photographic practice to experiment with how
meaning is constructed through framing, light, time, sequencing, and the manipulation
of images.
As students progress through Years 12 and 13, they are taught to generate, refine,
and present a coherent body of work in response to a proposition. Through iterative
investigation, critical reflection, and engagement with established practice, students
develop increasing technical control and increasingly sustained studio practice,
artistic agency, and critical judgement, enabling them to communicate ideas through
resolved photographic imagery.

  Visual Arts – Photography leads to pathways in creative and cultural industries,
  including photography, digital content creation, film and media production,
  creative technologies, and gallery and museum practice.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Visual Arts – Photography, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to analyse established practice and communicate the creative ideas, processes, intentions, and meanings in their own
 and others’ artwork.

 Responsible use of artificial intelligence
 Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues relating to
 ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking, source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-making. Responsible AI use
 emphasises the importance of exercising independent judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent about AI use, considering diverse
 perspectives, and developing independent thinking.
